 Lieutenant General K R Rao retired / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Oct 22, 2026, 14:35 IST Comments Share AA + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 The 8th Central Pay Commission has an opportunity to resolve existing pay and pension anomalies affecting the Armed Forces. It must address unresolved issues from prior commissions to prevent further litigation and expenditures. A permanent mechanism should be established to ensure timely and reasoned decisions are made on anomalies. Financial scrutiny should facilitate lawful resolutions without excessive delays obstructing the process. BMP-2K of the army firing at night during a training exercise. (Image credit: Indian Army) The 8th Central Pay Commission (CPC) offers a rare opportunity to correct longstanding pay and pension anomalies, particularly those affecting the Armed Forces. It must address not only future revision but also unresolved legacies of earlier commissions. Otherwise, the same disputes will generate representations, litigation, and avoidable expenditure for another decade. The volume of pay and pension cases points to institutional failure. Administrative delay—and appeals against relief granted by the Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT) and other courts—often forces veterans into prolonged litigation for legitimate dues. When I took over as ADG PS in 2005, I appeared before the Delhi High Court in connection with some 1,600 pending pension cases. The AFT, established in 2008, was intended to provide specialised adjudication and reduce the burden on conventional courts. Yet departments still contest decisions of the tribunal created to provide timely redress. The controversy over Major Generals drawing lower pay and pension than subordinate Brigadiers is not merely an arithmetic error. It exposes weaknesses in Pay Commission implementation and in the machinery for resolving anomalies. 1. Break the cycle, not just the pay scale Successive Pay Commissions revise pay structures, but anomalies often surface years later through promotions, increments, allowances, and pension calculations. The 8th CPC should audit unresolved issues inherited from the 4th through 7th CPCs and adopt a simple rule: no anomaly from one commission should become the next commission’s liability. A permanent, empowered mechanism should identify each case, determine its cause and financial effect, assign responsibility and order time-bound correction. It should also test proposed pay structures against promotion and pension scenarios before implementation, so predictable distortions are prevented rather than litigated. 2. A closed committee does not close an anomaly Anomaly committees commonly expire within a limited implementation window, while many defects emerge only after later promotions or pension revisions. Files are then treated as closed or deferred to the next Pay Commission. Unresolved issues inherited from the 4th and 5th CPCs still demanded attention; similar concerns, including Military Service Pay and pay fixation, followed even after the 7th CPC. The Symbolic opening slide presented to the 6th CPC, showing how unresolved anomalies were carried forward from earlier Pay Commissions. An anomaly does not disappear when the committee examining it is dissolved. Responsibility must continue until every registered issue receives a reasoned decision. 3. Scrutiny must not become a veto by delay Financial scrutiny is essential, but it must facilitate lawful decisions rather than obstruct them indefinitely. Service Headquarters may identify an anomaly and send a proposal to the Ministry of Defence, only for repeated objections and differing interpretations to keep the file circulating for years. Frequent changes in senior military appointments weaken continuity and institutional memory. Successive officers must reconstruct old cases, while finance authorities retain familiarity with the correspondence and precedents. Both sides therefore need a common digital case record, named responsibility and enforceable timelines. Genuine differences deserve reasoned resolution, but settled issues should not be repeatedly reopened. MoD Finance must be accountable for timely, consistent decisions, just as Service Headquarters must submit complete, evidence-based proposals. Financial propriety cannot mean administrative paralysis. 4. Litigation ss the costliest form of economy The aggregate cost of correction must be assessed, but it cannot determine whether an established anomaly is lawful. Delay may enlarge the liability through arrears, interest, legal expenses, and retrospective implementation. Every proposal should therefore compare the cost of correction with the cost and risk of inaction. The government must distinguish legitimate appeals from repetitive litigation over settled principles. When a final judgment clearly applies to a defined class, the Ministry should examine extending relief to similarly situated personnel and amend the rules where necessary. A central register of significant AFT, High Court and Supreme Court decisions on pay and pensions would promote consistent implementation and prevent departments from relitigating the same question. 5. Veterans should not have to sue for their dues Prolonged litigation imposes financial and emotional costs on veterans, some of whom exhaust savings or die before receiving relief. The government meanwhile incurs legal and administrative expenses, while courts revisit disputes that could have been resolved administratively. The result is inequitable: those able to litigate may obtain relief, while similarly placed veterans remain excluded. When recurring pay-fixation and pension issues drive retired officers to court, the damage extends beyond individual grievances to confidence in the administration. A veteran should not have to become a litigant to obtain an entitlement already recognised for an equivalent class. It is quite absurd. 6. Six reforms the 8th CPC must deliver First, create a permanent Pay Anomaly Resolution Cell. Include Service Headquarters, MoD Finance, the Department of Expenditure, and pension authorities; maintain a live register, assign owners, and impose deadlines. Second, apply settled judicial principles consistently. Review comparable cases after final judgments and issue general instructions wherever legally justified. Third, use data to detect errors. CGDA and pension authorities should analyse digitised service and pension records, including SPARSH, to flag recurring discrepancies and enable lawful batch correction. Fourth, make delay visible and accountable. Every representation should have a designated authority, a decision deadline and a recorded explanation for delay or appeal. Fifth, prevent unintended pay inversion. Stress-test pay fixation, increments, MSP, and pension rules so that senior officers do not draw less than juniors in comparable circumstances, except where lawful differences justify it. Sixth, add an independent escalation route. Cases unresolved beyond the deadline should automatically reach a higher interdepartmental body empowered to decide—not merely return—the file. An annual public report on pending anomalies, disposal times, appeals and compliance with judgments would provide the transparency needed to turn these safeguards into practice. Correct the system, not just the judgment The 8th CPC must do more than prescribe revised pay scales. It must repair the institutional weaknesses that allow anomalies to survive successive commissions. MoD Finance must safeguard public expenditure through scrutiny that is timely, consistent, and informed by military-service realities; Service Headquarters must preserve continuity and pursue legitimate cases effectively. Accountability must be institutional, not rhetorical. Every reference to MoD Finance should identify the officer responsible, the date received, the objections raised, the deadline for decision and the authority empowered to resolve an impasse. Repeated return of a file without a reasoned order should not count as disposal. Unexplained delay, inconsistent interpretation, and avoidable appeals must be reviewed at a senior level and reported annually. Finance should be judged not only by expenditure restrained, but also by lawful entitlements delivered on time and liabilities avoided through prompt correction. The success of the 8th CPC should be measured not only by the pay structure it creates, but by the legacy disputes it resolves, the new anomalies it prevents and the trust it restores. The choice is stark: correct the system now, or condemn another generation of veterans to chase files, fund litigation, and wait for justice. Public money deserves vigilance; those who served the nation deserve fairness—and both demand accountable decisions, not bureaucratic silence. About the Author Lieutenant General K R Rao retired Lieutenant General K R Rao (retired) is an alumnus of Sainik School Korukonda, National Defence Academy, Defence Services Staff College, College of Defence Management and National Defence College New Delhi. He is a double M Phil in Defence studies, International Affairs and Masters In Management Studies from Osmania University. He has served in high altitude areas of Siachen, Nathula, deserts of Rajasthan, Plains of Punjab and jungles of Assam. He commanded an Artillery Regiment in the J&K, an Armoured Artillery Brigade in Deserts and an Artillery Division in Plains of Punjab. He has commanded the School of Artillery and finally retired as the Director General of Artillery. He had taken part in 1971 War at Kargil and Operation Pawan in Sri Lanka in 1987. Read More
